solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hold up popular bird at Christmas

blocks.note: to hold up a bank is to rob it

explanation.surface: A festive cheer for the robin, the bird of every Christmas card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' reads as 'display' beside a bird; it is the robber's hold-up. The robin is the British Christmas bird, the redbreast on cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin is the bird most associated with Christmas in Britain.

clue.text: After frolic around Kansas, prepares to go home?

indicators.note: KS is placed after the reversed frolic
turns CAPER round to REPAC

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker who has had fun in Kansas starts packing for the journey home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around Kansas' looks like travelling about the state; 'around' actually turns the frolic back to front, and 'After' puts KS at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone going home packs their bags again: repacks. The question mark flags this as one example.

clue.text: Wash black articles

blocks.note: the two English articles, A and THE

explanation.surface: Laundry advice: wash your black items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests clothing beside 'black' and 'wash'; it means the grammatical articles, a and the.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to bathe something is to wash it, as with a wound.

clue.text: Writer making one afraid of Christmas?

blocks.note: a coward is one who is afraid

explanation.surface: A whimsical question: is there a writer who could make someone scared of Christmas?
explanation.walkthrough: Noël Coward was the English playwright and songwriter; read literally, his name is a person afraid of Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the author of Private Lives and Blithe Spirit wrote plays, songs and diaries.

clue.text: Translated from Arabic, one sort of exercise

indicators.note: translating turns words into different forms, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A phrase translated from Arabic turns out to mean one kind of exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated from Arabic' sounds like a language note, but only the letters of ARABIC and ONE matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaerobic exercise is short intense effort, such as sprinting or weightlifting.

clue.text: Hating cereal is out of character

explanation.surface: Someone who normally loves breakfast suddenly hating cereal is behaving unlike themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts 'out of character' about a person's odd breakfast; the phrase is really the definition of the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that goes against the grain runs contrary to one's nature.

clue.text: Scientists in stasis roused to accept award thus

indicators.note: stirred up, so the letters of STASIS are mixed
the rearranged STASIS takes in TROPHY and SIC

explanation.surface: Dormant scientists are woken up to go and collect a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin 'sic', familiar from '[sic]' in quotations, means thus. 'Scientists in' looks like part of the picture, but 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrophysicists are scientists who study stars and space.

clue.text: Very odd choice

blocks.note: the adjective: excellent, of the finest quality

explanation.surface: A comment that someone has made a very strange choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Choice' reads as a noun, a selection; here it is the adjective meaning fine or excellent, as in 'a rare treat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare means uncommon to the point of oddity, and also exceptionally fine, as choice does.

clue.text: Bishop, getting fit, is shot in part of church

blocks.note: to have a shot is to have a try

explanation.surface: A bishop getting into shape is photographed inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting fit' and 'shot' suggest exercise and photography; they are APT and TRY. The baptistry is where the font stands, used for baptisms.
explanation.definitionFit: A baptistry is the part of a church set aside for baptism.

clue.text: Bank worker gets sack

blocks.note: the verb: to dismiss in disgrace, especially from the armed forces

explanation.surface: A bank employee is fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' reads as a noun, maybe a bag of cash; it is the verb, to dismiss, and cashier has that sense too.
explanation.definitionFit: A cashier handles money in a bank; to cashier someone is to dismiss them in disgrace.

clue.text: Old man in mine, he can’t work after an hour

indicators.note: 'after' in its sense of 'following in order', so the work is written down behind the hour

blocks.note: a coal mine is a pit

explanation.surface: An old miner, past his shift, laments that he can no longer work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is not an elderly man but a very old kind of man: Pithecanthropus is the former name of Java Man, an early human.
explanation.definitionFit: Pithecanthropus, the 'ape-man', is an early human ancestor, so an old man in the prehistoric sense.

clue.text: Volume changes, namely by finale in adapted score

indicators.note: 'by' in its sense of 'next to', so namely stands right beside the finale
SC END goes inside the rearranged SCORE
changed, so the letters of SCORE are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musical score is reworked so that its volume shifts, especially in the finale.
explanation.walkthrough: SC, short for Latin scilicet, is used in text to mean namely. The musical surface hides that 'score' is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term used as a plain definition: each one is a gradual swell in loudness, a change of volume.

clue.text: Note short skirt

indicators.note: cut short, so MINIM loses its last letter

blocks.note: a minim is a musical note (a half note); 'short' docks its final M

explanation.surface: A reminder to notice a skirt's short length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short skirt' looks like a phrase describing the answer; 'short' belongs with 'Note' and cuts MINIM down.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortened word: the answer is the everyday clipping of miniskirt, the 1960s fashion.

clue.text: One seeking water wings or odd flaps

indicators.note: a flap is a commotion, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: A bird looking for water, flapping its wings or doing something odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water wings' leaps out as the armbands for swimmers, but the definition stops at 'water'; 'flaps' is the verb that stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowsing rod is the forked stick a dowser uses to seek underground water.

clue.text: Blubber — from whales, obviously

indicators.note: the answer is taken from inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Blubber comes from whales, which goes without saying.
explanation.walkthrough: Blubber is whale fat in the surface, but here it is the verb, to cry noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to blubber is to weep noisily and without restraint.

clue.text: Much food and drink, but not a place to sit

indicators.note: tells you to remove an A from TEA

blocks.note: a banquet is a lavish meal

explanation.surface: A feast with lots to eat and drink but nowhere to sit down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a place to sit' reads as a complaint; split it, 'not a' strips TEA and 'place to sit' is the definition. A banquette is an upholstered bench seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A banquette is a long cushioned bench, especially along a wall in a restaurant.

clue.text: Who, say, follows what, say, magician?

indicators.note: 'follows' in its sense of 'comes after in sequence', so the Who example goes second
'say' asks for a sound: WHICH, a word for what, is spoken as WITCH

blocks.note: which = what, as in 'which one?'; sounds like WITCH
Doctor Who, the TV time traveller: the Doctor is an example of a Who

explanation.surface: A riddle about question words, one following another, that ends in a magician.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'say's do different jobs: the first means 'for example' (Who, the BBC Doctor), the second means spoken aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the healer of some traditional societies is credited with magic powers, so a kind of magician.

clue.text: No Christmas crackers for fans of the royals

indicators.note: crackers means crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: Royalists are denied Christmas crackers, the paper tubes that bang at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christmas crackers' is a British table tradition, but here 'crackers' means crazy and scrambles NO CHRISTMAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose paraphrase: supporters of kingship as a system are, in practice, fans of the royal family.

clue.text: Can East in West show?

indicators.note: TIN E is placed inside MAE

explanation.surface: A question about whether an eastern act can play in the West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East' and 'West' look like a matching pair of compass points; only East is. West is Mae West, the Hollywood star, whose first name wraps TIN E.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: an afternoon performance at a theatre or cinema is one kind of show.

clue.text: The old soldier’s first, of course

indicators.note: take only the first letter of soldier

blocks.note: ye = the, in old spelling ('Ye Olde Shoppe')

explanation.surface: Of course the veteran soldier came first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old soldier' reads as a veteran; the phrase splits into 'The old' (YE) and the soldier's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Of course!' and 'Yes!' are both emphatic agreement.

clue.text: That entered after coming out

blocks.note: the surface reads a door or room, somewhere physically walked into; the setter means a social world one joins
not leaving a place: 'coming out' is a debutante's formal presentation to fashionable circles

explanation.surface: Something paradoxically entered only after leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante's 'coming out' was her formal introduction to fashionable society, so coming out is how one enters it.
explanation.definitionFit: High society is what a debutante joins when she comes out.

clue.text: So good to escape gangsters

indicators.note: to escape is to get out, so the good letter leaves the gangsters

explanation.surface: Relief that the good guy has got away from the mobsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So good' reads as praise; 'So' is the definition, alone at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus and so both mean 'therefore' or 'in this way'.

clue.text: Tipsy concierge drinking Tango in vain

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters of CONCIERGE stagger into a new order
the rearranged letters take in T

explanation.surface: A drunk hotel porter sipping a Tango, an orange fizzy drink, to no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In vain' reads as 'uselessly'; 'in' is only a link and 'vain' the definition. Tango is also a British soft drink, which makes 'drinking' fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Egocentric means self-centred, close to vain.

clue.text: Power shower, you might say?

indicators.note: points to how the word is spoken

explanation.surface: A power shower, the strong kind in a bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power shower' is a bathroom fitting; split it, and 'Power' is the definition and 'shower' the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as nouns or verbs: royal rule is sovereign power, and to rule is to hold power.

clue.text: Post-punk fan caught with heroin

explanation.surface: A post-punk music fan is arrested with drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Goth grew out of post-punk music in the early 1980s, and its fans are goths.
explanation.definitionFit: A goth is a follower of the gothic rock scene that came out of post-punk.

clue.text: 1950s Britain saw this state funeral?

blocks.note: compulsory military service ran in Britain until 1960
a funeral service held by the nation

explanation.surface: A history question about a grand state funeral in postwar Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: National Service was Britain's peacetime conscription, ending in 1960. The question mark marks the second sense as whimsical: a state funeral is a service for the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: National Service is the name for British conscription, which young men served through the 1950s.

clue.text: Footballer backing county they never forget

indicators.note: going backwards, so PELE is reversed

blocks.note: Hants is the abbreviation for Hampshire, an English county

explanation.surface: A footballer loyally supporting his county's fans, who never forget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as supporting; it reverses PELE. Hants for Hampshire comes from its old name, Hantescire.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying goes that an elephant never forgets.

clue.text: Capital letters dyslexic starts with

indicators.note: the letters at the start of dyslexic

blocks.note: the first of the two letters that open dyslexic
'with' = and, joining the two letters, written out as a word
the second of the opening pair, dy-

explanation.surface: Upper-case letters that someone with dyslexia begins with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital letters' reads as upper case; 'Capital' alone is the definition, the old British 'capital!' meaning excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital and dandy are both old-fashioned words for excellent.
